Bloom Energy has reported strong demand for its fuel cell systems tied to AI data centers, raised its 2026 revenue forecast, and secured attention through links to Oracle's Project Jupiter contract and renewed AI infrastructure spending.

The real story is the growing need for on-site power as data centers strain local grids, which directly aligns with Bloom Energy's core business of providing fuel cell based electricity solutions for power hungry AI facilities.

We will now look at how Bloom Energy's AI driven data center demand story could shape the broader investment narrative from here.

Explore the AI energy sector beyond Bloom Energy by identifying power-hungry data center suppliers already gaining attention with 41 power grid technology and infrastructure stocks

Bloom Energy Investment Narrative Recap

To own Bloom Energy, you need to buy into a simple idea. Data centers and other power hungry facilities need reliable on site electricity when local grids are already stretched. According to JRY, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the main ceiling on Bloom's opportunity is buyer awareness, not technology or execution. The short term swing factor now is whether AI driven projects actually convert into orders and installations at the pace implied by the raised 2026 revenue outlook.

The biggest operational risk in the near term is that financing costs, project delays and permitting challenges slow those deployments while the stock remains highly volatile. Any pause in AI infrastructure spending or regulatory friction would likely weigh on new fuel cell installations. On top of that, recent shareholder dilution and significant insider selling add another layer of risk around how Bloom funds growth if external borrowing already makes up all liabilities.

The clearest catalyst tied to the latest move in Bloom Energy is the raised full year 2026 revenue forecast linked to AI data center demand. That guidance sits on top of very strong recent execution, with revenue of US$3.83b and earnings shifting from low margins to a 13.5% net margin, supported by high quality earnings. Forward looking estimates currently point to revenue growth of 32.1% a year and earnings growth near 39.7% a year.

This outlook only matters if Bloom can keep converting AI interest into contracted projects and installed fuel cell systems at scale. JRY argues that the product is ready and the constraint is institutional inertia, which puts execution squarely on sales cycles, permitting and buyer education. Investors also need to weigh valuation signals, including a P/E of 95.9x and an internal DCF view that suggests the stock trades about 51.5% below estimated future cash flow value, alongside continued share price volatility.

Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, used the November 20 episode of his podcast, The Real Eisman Playbook, to argue that the AI market has changed: "Without Nvidia backstopping the AI stack, AI is no longer one trade. And that's why stock picking is back, and valuation is back."

Shutterstock

Three days later, the board of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock rose 32.36% in today's session. Does his return undo Eisman's thesis? The price data suggests the split he described had already happened.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Why Eisman Says NVIDIA Held the AI Trade Together

Eisman's argument centers on circular financing. He said Huang took equity stakes in, or lent money to, companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, CoreWeave and Nebius Group, and those companies then used the money to buy NVIDIA chips. "He created, I think, a virtual vertical holding company," Eisman said. When one balance sheet supports the whole network, having any AI stock means having a piece of the same machine. Once that support passes, Eisman said, the companies "need to be evaluated on their own merits and not as part of a larger whole."

Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) stock is up 12.5% as of 1:05 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 23, after news broke that Jensen Huang had returned to Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were up 4.8% and 6.4%, respectively.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Oracle stock rallies as Jensen Huang returns

In a surprise announcement this morning, Nvidia's board said it has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president, and board member. This comes roughly two weeks after his departure and just days after the board told investors it did not intend to reinstate him. However, the board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government" and that, based on that input, it was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Huang has been instrumental in shaping the AI industry, and his return helped lift stocks across the AI trade, like Oracle.

Oracle says its OpenAI deal is fully funded

At the same time, Oracle reassured investors on Friday that the company had secured the financing necessary to fulfill its contract with OpenAI. Oracle also said its massive Abilene data center campus, which OpenAI has already used, is nearly complete. That's critical given the company's cash flow crunch: It spent about $5 billion more on capital investments last quarter than its operations brought in.

Tech stocks surge as Nvidia rally adds $2 trillion to Nasdaq 100

US technology stocks staged a broad rally Monday, with gains across chipmakers, AI infrastructure providers and software companies adding nearly $2 trillion to the Nasdaq 100's market capitalization as investors welcomed Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD).

The chipmaker was up 32%, making it the strongest performer among major US technology stocks, with shares reaching an intraday high of $171.50.

The rally extended well beyond Nvidia, with investors also piling into companies tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.

Dell Technologies Inc (NASDAQ:DELL) jumped 22%, while AI cloud providers Nebius and CoreWeave each gained 21%. Memory makersMicron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU) rose 19%, Marvell Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MRVL) added 18%, and Arm Holdings PLC (NASDAQ:ARM) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (ADR) (NYSE:TSM) each advanced 16%.

Storage companies also enjoyed strong gains, with Western Digital up 15%, Seagate Technology and SanDisk both rising 14%, and Intel gaining 14%.

Oracle Corp (NYSE:ORCL, XETRA:ORC) climbed 12%, as did Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA), while Palantir Technologies Inc (NYSE:PLTR) added 10%. Qualcomm Inc (NASDAQ:QCOM, XETRA:QCI) rose 10%, Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD, XETRA:AMD) gained 8%, and Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO, XETRA:1YD) advanced 3%.

The scale of the move suggests Huang's return has done more than remove a leadership concern at Nvidia. It has also renewed investor confidence in the broader AI investment cycle, which has come under pressure amid questions over infrastructure spending, financing arrangements and the returns on massive capital commitments.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said Huang's return demonstrated his influence over both Nvidia and the wider AI sector.

She described him as the "godfather of AI", arguing that he has a talismanic influence on the industry and that his reinstatement also shifts the dial for corporate finance.

Brooks noted that Nvidia's board had concluded it could not see a future for the company without its co-founder, despite the serious questions surrounding his departure barely two weeks earlier.

For investors, however, the leadership question is only part of the story.

Antonio Di Giacomo, senior market analyst at XS.com, said the scale of Nvidia's gains highlighted how heavily uncertainty surrounding its leadership had weighed on the stock.

Analysts at BMO and Goldman Sachs also welcomed Huang's return, although questions remain about Nvidia's investment strategy and its exposure to other AI companies.

title: Oracle’s Larry Ellison just lost $10.9 billion and fell from the top 10 richest billionaires in the world after his cloud company’s stock tanks
detail:
Oracle’s Larry Ellison just lost $10.9 billion and fell from the top 10 richest billionaires in the world after his cloud company’s stock tanks
A recent drop in Oracle shares sent Larry Ellison’s fortune tumbling down the ultra-rich list past Walmart heirs Jim Walton, Rob Walton, and Alice Walton. · Fortune · Bloomberg / Contributor / Getty Images
Emma Burleigh
Mon, November 23, 2026 at 10:00 AM MST 3 min read
ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Like many other tech billionaires, Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison is no stranger to how a stock market swing can make or cost him billions—and he just took a  nearly $11 billion hit that knocked him from the top 10 richest billionaires.

Ellison's net worth dropped $10.9 billion at the close of markets last Friday, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as his cloud company's shares continued to drop. 

Oracle's stock fell around 7.5% to around $102 at the end of last week, the lowest it's been since January 2024, as the company's shares have slid 47% year-over-year.

It's a far cry from when the business' stock hit a peak of $345 in September 2025 amid surging demand for AI computing power; but in the following year, investors have grown concerned over Oracle's massive AI infrastructure spending, mounting debt, and negative free cash flow. As Ellison owns around 40% of the company, those losses hit his pocket hard, sending him tumbling down the ultra-rich list past Walmart heirs Jim Walton, Rob Walton, and Alice Walton. 

However, Ellison still has a whopping $139 billion to his name—enough to put him thousands of times above the estimated $62 million net-worth threshold for America's wealthiest 0.1% of households. 

Even a multibillion-dollar loss barely makes a dent in a fortune of that size. And this isn't the first time the 82-year-old has had his wealth swing dramatically from one week to the next.

Fortune reached out to Oracle for comment. 

Billionaire fortunes are at the whim of the stock market 

For most billionaires whose fortunes are tied to company stock, a single rally can send their net worth soaring by billions. However, a sudden sell-off or market change can wipe out just as much wealth almost overnight.

In September 2025, Ellison briefly took the throne as the richest person in the world, outstripping Tesla billionaire Elon Musk, who had steadily held the spot for nearly a year straight. Following better-than-expected quarterly results, the Oracle cofounder subsequently enjoyed a $101 billion surge in wealth overnight, hitting a $393 billion net worth—which placed him ahead of Musk's $385 billion fortune at the time. 

But Ellison's ranking as the world's richest person last year was short-lived: His estimated net worth fell by $34 billion in the two days following Oracle's stock surge, according to Bloomberg's index. J. Bradford DeLong, a U.C. Berkeley economist, told Fortune that the sharp downfall was triggered by "second thoughts" around Oracle's cloud deal with OpenAI.
